heading: What this is
body: Solar Policy Explorer scores countries, states and provinces against the Electric Protocol - a set of policy questions asking how easy it is for ordinary homes and businesses to generate, store and sell their own power.

heading: The questions
body: Questions are grouped into topic groups. Each question has an impact score (how much it counts toward the total) and a small set of possible answers describing what is actually in place. Answers run from weak to strong - some questions have two, others three - and are labelled Weak, Developed or Strong, best first.

heading: Score
body: A jurisdiction's score is the weighted share of what is in place, among the questions that have actually been answered - then scaled down by how much of the questionnaire has been answered overall. This means a jurisdiction cannot rank highly by only answering a handful of its best questions; broad, honest coverage beats a few cherry-picked answers. Scores are shown as a rating of one to five suns, with the percentage alongside for those who want the detail.

heading: Questions answered
body: A separate measure from score: the share of questions answered at all, regardless of how they scored. A jurisdiction with too little data shows as "not enough data" rather than a score, so a lack of research is never mistaken for bad policy.

heading: Evidence
body: Every answer needs a real source - a law, a regulator decision, a market operator's own data, or a published report - shown with the answer so you can follow it up. Web addresses in the evidence are links that open in a new tab.

heading: Spotted an error?
body: Use "Suggest a correction" on any answer: choose the answer you think is right, add your evidence (a link, or the name of a report), say what it shows, and give your name. A reviewer checks it before anything changes. If a question is missing, use "Propose a new policy question" on a country's page - once accepted, it counts toward every country's score.

heading: Reports
body: "Download Policy Summary Report" on a country's page opens a preview of an accessible PDF that you can read, search and download. Nothing is sent anywhere - it is made in your browser.

heading: Jurisdictions
body: Most rows are countries. Where policy varies a lot within a country (such as the US, Australia or Canada), it is shown as its states or provinces instead, since one national score would hide too much. The European Union is shown as one consolidated row on the scoreboard, though every member still has its own jurisdiction page.
